part_title: Choosing Inference Modes — Real-Time, Batch, Asynchronous, Serverless and Edge
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 slides 52–53 visually inspected; diagrams, examples, labels and calculations reviewed against the approved beginner visual-first narration standard.

scenes.title: Choose an inference mode
scenes.narration: Inference is the moment a trained model applies learned patterns to new information to make a prediction. Start with the top-right diagram: new input travels into a trained model and a result comes out. This is different from training, when the model learns from examples. Across the slide are four deployment choices. Real-time inference on the far left responds to individual requests with low latency, meaning the time between sending a request and getting an answer is short. The diagram shows a chatbot response and a fraud check, where the customer might be actively waiting. Next is batch inference, where many records are processed offline as one job. Follow the arrow from input files to Amazon S3, to a batch prediction process and then output results. A business could score millions of customers every night without keeping an endpoint waiting for each request. The third column is asynchronous inference. A single request that may take longer is accepted, queued and processed, and the result becomes available later. The illustration includes a queue such as S Q S, though the exact backend depends on the service and architecture. Video or large-document processing can fit this pattern. The fourth column shows serverless inference for intermittent demand. A managed service allocates capacity as needed, but supported model and container limitations, startup delay and pricing rules still matter. Do not treat all four modes as interchangeable. At the bottom, the factors are latency, throughput, cost and workload pattern. The worked example chooses real-time fraud scoring while each transaction is happening, alongside nightly batch scoring for all customers. Neither mode is inherently more accurate: both may apply the same trained model. Ask yourself: if a report can arrive tomorrow and contains ten million records, why pay for an instant response for every record? Batch inference may be the better choice.

scenes.title: Inference at the edge
scenes.narration: This slide compares using a model near the data source with sending data to a remote server. At the left, a user asks to summarize some text. The arrow leads to an edge device shown as a compact computing board. An edge device is a local computer, phone, sensor system or embedded board that can do processing close to where data originates. Here a small language model, S L M, is shown running locally. It may use fewer computing resources, respond quickly and, if designed for it, work without an internet connection. This can be useful when connectivity is unreliable or keeping data on the device is important. Now follow the arrow toward the cloud icon and remote server on the right. A larger language model, L L M, may offer more capabilities for complex instructions but usually requires a network request, adding latency and potential cost. The large server picture represents remote computation; the final arrow points to a response. This flow should not be interpreted as requiring every edge task to call the cloud. A local model may answer completely on its own, or an application can selectively send a request to the cloud when more capability is needed. Look at the four bottom callouts: low latency, smaller footprint, offline capability and optional cloud support. The decision depends on available memory, processing power, data privacy, network reliability, model quality and business needs. A warehouse scanner that must operate during an internet outage may favor local inference, while an occasional complex document summary could be routed to a cloud model. The image shows a combined design rather than a universal rule. Check: is a small model automatically less secure or more accurate than a large model? No. Security and quality depend on design, data, controls and evaluation.
